# How to Get Your Product Mentioned by ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity

Author: Shiva Dhali (@dhalishiva)

Source: https://x.com/dhalishiva/status/2116581489244807373

[中文全文](../如何让AI提及你的产品_ShivaDhali_2116581489244807373.md)

Someone asks ChatGPT "what's the best tool for X?" It names three products. Yours isn't one of them.

They never Google it. They never see your landing page. You never even knew you lost the sale.

That's the new search problem. Ranking #1 on Google matters less when the answer is written for the user before they click anything.

So I dug into the research on what actually gets a product mentioned by ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI answers. Some of it is obvious. Some of it flips old SEO advice upside down.

## The data: clicks are disappearing

Most searches already end without a click. SparkToro, using Similarweb data, found 68% of US Google searches ended without a click in January–April 2026, up from about 60% in 2024.

AI summaries cut clicks roughly in half. Pew Research tracked 900 US adults across 68,879 Google searches in March 2025:

- Users clicked a regular result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, vs 15% without one

- They clicked a link inside the summary just 1% of the time

- 26% ended their browsing session after an AI summary, vs 16% without

AI pulls from a small set of sources. Semrush studied 100M+ citations across ChatGPT search, Google AI Mode and Perplexity from July to October 2025:

- Reddit and Wikipedia were among the most-cited domains on every platform

- Google AI Mode leaned on LinkedIn (cited in nearly 15% of responses), YouTube and Google's own properties

- ChatGPT's sources shifted sharply in mid-September: Reddit fell from about 60% of responses to about 10%, while Forbes, Medium and PR Newswire gained

That last point matters. What AI cites can change in weeks. There's no "rank once and relax" anymore.

## What actually gets you cited

The best research on this is a paper called "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" from Princeton and IIT Delhi researchers, published at KDD 2024. They tested which content changes make AI engines quote a page more.

What worked:

- Cite your sources: add references to credible sources

- Add quotations: include real quotes from relevant people

- Add statistics: swap vague claims for specific numbers

These three gave roughly a 30–40% relative boost in how visible a page was inside AI answers. On Perplexity, adding statistics improved how prominently a page was presented by up to 37%.

What didn't work: keyword stuffing. The classic SEO trick showed little to no improvement, and on Perplexity it did worse than doing nothing.

The lesson flips old SEO on its head. You don't write for a crawler matching words. You write for a model deciding what's worth quoting. Facts, numbers and sources win.

## What the big names say

Sundar Pichai, Google CEO, to The Verge's Nilay Patel at Google I/O, May 2024: AI Overviews give people "jumping-off points, and so they engage more." He also admitted the risk: "If people over time don't see value, website owners don't see value coming back from Google, I think we'll pay a price."

Rand Fishkin, SparkToro co-founder and the person behind the zero-click data above, in an April 2026 Search Engine Land interview: zero-click search started around 2011, long before generative AI. He also notes AI answers vary run to run, so you should test many prompts and look for patterns, not trust one result.

Tibo, indie SaaS founder, in a recent X post: "organic traffic from Google goes to zero but you need SEO to get mentioned by AI." His advice: "be where the AI goes: Reddit, X articles, blog listicles."

Google's CEO is optimistic, the data person is skeptical, the builder is practical. All three agree on one thing: visibility now means being in the answer, not just the results.

## The playbook

Seven moves any builder can start this week:

- Ask the AIs first. Prompt ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google with the questions your buyers ask: "best tool for X", "alternatives to Y". Note who gets named. Run each a few times, since answers vary.

- Write pages that answer one exact question. "How to detect duplicate invoices" beats "Our Features." AI quotes answers, not brochures.

- Pack pages with facts. Real numbers, named sources, short quotes. That's what the GEO study found moves the needle.

- Get mentioned where AI reads. Reddit threads, LinkedIn posts, YouTube, comparison listicles. Be genuinely helpful there, because communities spot ads fast.

- Show up in "best X" lists. Many AI answers about tools lean on roundup articles. Reach out to the people who write them.

- Keep classic SEO alive. AI search tools still pull from the web, so pages that rank and load fast still matter.

- Recheck monthly. ChatGPT's top sources shifted in a matter of weeks in 2025. What worked last quarter may not now.

What not to do:

- Don't keyword-stuff. It didn't help in the GEO study, and hurt on Perplexity.

- Don't spam Reddit. Fake reviews and sock-puppet accounts get banned, and they wreck trust when caught.

- Don't write fake "best tools" lists that crown yourself #1 with nothing to back it up. If it reads like an ad, people (and maybe models) will treat it like one.

## My take

SEO isn't dead. It's just not the finish line anymore.

The goal used to be "rank on page one." Now it's "be the name the AI says." And the way you get there is old-school: say useful things, back them with real numbers, and be present where people actually talk.

The good news for small builders: an AI doesn't care how big your ad budget is. It cares whether your page answers the question.

Have u ever asked ChatGPT about ur own product? What did it say? 👀
